To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the magnitude of prey response to chemical cues is a saturating function of the amount of prey biomass consumed by predators.
prey growth responses are an asymptotic function to the number and biomass of prey consumed, and that the magnitude of the asymptote increases with increasing prey number consumed.
prey growth rate is an asymptotic response to predation risk that is stronger when more prey are eaten, but not necessarily stronger when more biomass is consumed.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the relationship between predator-induced phenotypic plastic responses of prey and how prey perceive risk from predators.
how prey assess predation risk and the implications of that risk for prey growth.
the mechanisms by which organisms assess risk, which is a fundamental aspect of predator-prey interactions.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
prey responses to predator chemical cues are a function of the number of prey consumed, but not prey biomass consumed.
prey growth rates respond to predation cues in an asymptotic manner and this response depends on the number of prey deaths, not the biomass consumed.
the magnitude of the prey response to predator cues is an asymptotic, saturating function of prey biomass, and that the asymptotic level is higher when more individual prey are consumed.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the magnitude of a phenotypic response to predator cues depends on both the number and size of prey consumed.
prey respond to predation events in a dose dependent way, but that the response is more pronounced when more individuals are consumed.
the number and biomass of prey consumed by a predator can both influence prey response.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the number of prey consumed is a more appropriate measure of relative risk to predators for plastic responses of prey.
prey responses to predator cues should be measured in relation to the number and size of prey consumed by the predator.

when designing experiments to test the effect of predator chemical cues, it is important to manipulate both the number of prey consumed and the size of prey consumed to fully understand the relationship between prey responses to risk and predator consumption.
